 Understanding App Status: The Key to Navigating Rideshare Accident Claims in Texas How Insurance Coverage Shifts with Each Stage of a Rideshare Driver's Journey photo provided by contributor Author: Resident Contributor 4 min read 
 Copied 
 Follow Us A rideshare vehicle can be involved in a collision while the driver is off duty, waiting for a request, traveling to a pickup, or transporting a passenger. Texas insurance law treats those stages differently. The app's status at the time of impact can influence which policy responds and how much liability coverage must be available.
 Before discussing payment, an injured person needs to establish whether the driver was connected to the rideshare network and whether a trip had been accepted. Texas Insurance Code Chapter 1954 supplies the framework.
 When the App Is Off, the Rideshare Coverage Framework Changes
 A driver using a personal vehicle for an ordinary, offline journey is not in the same insurance period as someone available for platform requests. The personal automobile policy is the starting point for reviewing coverage, subject to its terms and exclusions.
 An app installed on a phone does not establish that the driver was working for a transportation network company. Nor does a rideshare sticker on a windshield prove an active trip. Investigators need the driver's actual connection status at the collision time, not the vehicle's past use.
 Waiting for a Ride Request Creates a Distinct Coverage Period
 Once a driver logs on and becomes available to receive requests, Texas law imposes specific insurance requirements even without a passenger or an accepted trip. Section 1954.052 requires at least $50,000 in bodily injury liability coverage per person, $100,000 per incident, and $25,000 in property damage liability coverage.
 This middle stage can complicate an insurance claim when the driver's account and the available records differ. For someone consulting a Houston rideshare accident attorney , the central question may be whether the driver was logged in and available at the instant of impact—not whether any fare had been earned that day. Establishing that distinction directs attention to the proper coverage requirements.
 Accepting a Request Changes the Insurance Position
 Texas defines a prearranged ride as beginning when the driver accepts a passenger's request through the company's digital network. A passenger does not have to be sitting inside the car for that period to begin. The drive toward the pickup location falls within the statutory definition.
 Under Section 1954.053, insurance during a prearranged ride must carry an aggregate liability limit of at least $1 million per incident for death, bodily injury, and property damage. That figure describes required coverage, not an automatic payment or a determination of fault. A claim still depends on collision evidence, documented losses, and policy terms.
 Passenger Drop-Off Marks Another Boundary
 Under the same statute, a prearranged ride ends when the last requesting rider leaves the driver's vehicle. If the driver remains online and available for another request, the requirements for the waiting period become relevant again.
 That creates a meaningful distinction between completing passenger transportation and disconnecting from the platform. Trip receipts, pickup and drop-off information, and company records can help identify the transition. The minutes around a pickup or drop-off deserve particular attention because a broad description such as “driving for a rideshare company” does not identify the legally relevant period.
 The Driver's Personal Insurer May Apply an Exclusion
 Texas law permits personal automobile insurers to exclude certain losses occurring while a driver is logged on or engaged in a prearranged ride. The Texas Department of Insurance also warns that most personal auto policies do not include coverage for rideshare work.
 However, the required rideshare insurance can be supplied by the driver, the company, or a combination. Section 1954.054 requires the company to provide the mandated coverage if the driver's qualifying insurance has lapsed or is insufficient. An insurer's denial therefore does not, by itself, establish that no coverage is available. The actual policies and statutory requirements must be compared.
 Platform Logs Offer More Than a Driver's Recollection
 Section 1954.154 requires transportation network companies and relevant insurers to assist in claim investigations by providing specified information. That includes precise log-on and log-off times during the 12 hours before and after a crash, along with a description of applicable coverage, exclusions, and limits.
 Those logs help establish whether a driver was connected to the network. Determining the exact trip stage may also require acceptance records, ride details, passenger receipts, and other available data. A timestamp records an event; it does not prove phone distraction or fault.
 Preserve the Records That Identify the Ride
 Evidence can become harder to locate as accounts change or records are no longer readily accessible. Injured riders and other motorists can retain information already in their possession, including:
 Ride receipts and booking confirmations, if applicable
 Screenshots of the driver's profile, vehicle details, and trip progress
 Messages or notifications connected to the ride
 Photographs, witness contact information, and crash-report details
 Communications from insurers or the rideshare company
 Keep original files whenever possible. A rider's receipt may confirm a booked journey, while a roadside witness may need other evidence to establish whether the driver was logged in.
 Coverage Status Does Not Decide Who Caused the Crash
 Higher insurance limits do not make a rideshare driver automatically responsible. App status determines which insurance requirements are relevant; liability still requires a separate assessment of driving conduct and the collision evidence. A different motorist's negligence may be central to the claim.
 Texas also addresses uninsured or underinsured motorist and personal injury protection coverage where the referenced statutory provisions require it. Availability and benefits require a review of the policies and circumstances, rather than assumptions based solely on an advertised liability limit.
 The Critical Detail Is the Moment of Impact
 A reliable rideshare accident claim begins with an exact timeline. Was the driver offline, online and waiting, responding to an accepted request, or carrying a passenger? The answer identifies the statutory insurance period but does not settle every other issue.
 Matching app records to crash evidence, policy documents, and the driver's account keeps the investigation focused on verifiable facts. In a claim involving several potential insurers, that precision can prevent a coverage dispute from obscuring the underlying injuries and losses.
